title: From Passive Accumulation to Active Transport: Transcytosis-Guided Nanomaterial Drug Delivery in Gastrointestinal Cancers
content: Nanomaterial-based drug delivery has traditionally relied on the enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect to explain preferential tumor accumulation. However, heterogeneous vascular permeability, inefficient tumor entry, and restricted intratumoral penetration continue to limit many nanomedicines. These limitations are especially relevant to gastrointestinal malignancies where abnormal vasculature, increased interstitial pressure, dense extracellular matrix and stromal cells provide sequential barriers to drug transport. Recent evidence indicates that active processes, including endothelial and intercellular transcytosis, may be important for nanomaterial transport. The most straightforward gastrointestinal example is pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, where recent studies have shown neuropilin-1-, caveolin-, Annexin A2-, and stimulus-mediated mechanisms for enhanced vascular crossing or deeper stromal penetration. Similar results in colorectal and hepatocellular carcinoma models point to wider applicability, but disease-specific data are patchy. This focused narrative review addresses the transition from passive accumulation to transport-informed design of nanomaterials, with emphasis on the distinction between entry into the vasculature and subsequent penetration into tissue. We argue that the future of gastrointestinal cancer nanomedicine lies not in replacing EPR with a single alternative mechanism, but in identifying the dominant transport bottleneck in individual tumors and engineering nanomaterials to navigate it in a measurable, biomarker-informed, and clinically tractable manner.
